text: You are an SRE assistant helping the on-call engineer investigate production incidents. Use the tools to query deployments, logs, metrics, configuration and runbooks. Be concise.

Hi, I'm Elena Duarte, on call this week. We just opened INC-20931, severity SEV-2: the payments-api checkout endpoint returns HTTP 502 for about 18% of requests since 14:07. Tomasz Wrona is the incident commander. One ground rule from Tomasz: no pod restarts in eu-west-1, the region is frozen for the PCI audit until Friday. Start with today's deployments of payments-api.

Three deployments today. The last one, v4.18.1, went out at 13:58, nine minutes before the first 502s, and it replaced the HTTP client that calls the card vault. That makes it the prime suspect. The two earlier releases only touched refunds, logging and dependencies. I suggest we look at the error logs next to confirm the errors come from the card vault calls.

Almost every error is the same: the card vault client's connection pool is exhausted, requests wait two seconds for a connection, time out, and the checkout returns a 502. It happens on every pod and in every region, so it's not a single bad node. A few slow fraud-scoring responses show up too, but they're warnings and don't fail requests.

The release removed the old HTTP client limits and introduced a pooled client. The new pool is much smaller than the previous connection limit, and it gives up after two seconds when no connection is free. Under checkout traffic the pool saturates, which is exactly what the logs show. Everything else in the diff is unchanged.
Open the card vault runbook.

name: readRunbook

text: The runbook is clear about this case: when a release changed the card vault client, roll it back first and don't tune pool sizes during the incident. It also says client-side pool exhaustion is usually a client configuration issue, not a vault outage, so there's no need to page the card vault team unless vault latency stays high after the rollback.
Before we decide anything: is the card vault itself healthy? Check its p99 latency.

The vault looks healthy: its p99 stays around 60 ms for the whole window, with no bump at 14:07. Requests that reach the vault are served normally. The problem is on our side: requests wait in the client's pool and never get a connection. That's consistent with what the runbook describes, and it means rolling back the client should be enough.
Show me one failing trace end to end, so I can paste it in the incident channel.

name: getTrace

text: Here's a typical one: the checkout spends 9 ms validating the cart and 31 ms on fraud scoring, then waits exactly 2,000 ms for a card vault connection, gives up, and returns a 502. The vault is never called. You can paste it as is; it shows the wait in the client pool very clearly.
Tomasz decided: we roll back to v4.18.0 instead of hotfixing the pool size, because a hotfix would need a full PCI review before it can ship. Please start the rollback.

Draft a short status update for #payments-incidents.

Status update, 14:34 UTC: Since 14:07, about 18% of checkouts fail with an error. The cause is identified: a configuration change in the 13:58 release of payments-api limits connections to the card vault. We are rolling back that release; recovery is expected around 15:00. Card data is not affected, and customers can retry their payment. Next update at 15:00 or when the rollback completes.
How bad is the customer impact so far?

Adding up the per-minute failures since 14:07, about 3,400 checkouts have failed so far, roughly 18% of the attempts. Before 14:07 the failure rate was at its usual level, a handful per minute. Most failed customers will retry, so the revenue loss is lower than the raw count, but finance will want this number for the postmortem.

What's the checkout 502 rate now?

Back to normal: the 502 ratio peaked around 18% between 14:07 and 14:57 and has been at about 0.1% since 14:59, which is our usual baseline. I'd keep the incident open for another 30 minutes before resolving it.
Draft the resolution message for the status page.

Resolved, 15:10 UTC: Between 14:07 and 14:58 UTC, some checkout attempts failed with an error. The issue was caused by a configuration change and was fixed by reverting it. Payments made during this period were not charged twice, and no card data was affected. If your payment failed, you can safely try again. We are sorry for the inconvenience.

How much of the monthly error budget did we burn?

name: getSlo

text: This incident used about 9 minutes of the 43-minute monthly budget for checkout availability. With the incident earlier this month, about 28 minutes remain, roughly 65%. That's above the 25% line where the policy freezes non-urgent releases, so releases can continue, but another incident of this size would bring us close.
Draft the timeline for the postmortem.

Timeline, all times UTC:
- 13:58 v4.18.1 deployed, replacing the card vault HTTP client with a pooled client.
- 14:07 first checkout 502s; the error ratio climbs to about 18%.
- 14:12 incident opened, on-call engineer starts the investigation.
- 14:16 logs show card vault pool exhaustion on every pod.
- 14:20 config diff confirms the new pool is much smaller than the previous limit.
- 14:31 decision to roll back rather than hotfix; rollback RB-5531 starts.
- 14:58 rollback complete.
- 14:59 502 ratio back to 0.1%.
Impact: checkout failures for 51 minutes. Detection was fast thanks to the 502 rate alert; the time to mitigation was mostly the rollback itself.
Suggest three action items.

1. Add an alert on card vault pool saturation (pending acquisitions), so we see the pool fill up before requests fail.
2. Load test client pool settings in staging with production-like checkout traffic before release.
3. Agree with compliance on a fast-track review for configuration-only hotfixes, so a hotfix is a real option next time instead of a full rollback.
Write the 'what went well / what went wrong' section.

What went well:
- The 502 rate alert fired within minutes, before customers reported anything.
- Logs, the config diff and the runbook pointed to the same cause in under fifteen minutes.
- The rollback worked as designed and needed no manual step.

What went wrong:
- The pool limit was chosen without a load test; staging traffic is too low to saturate it.
- Nothing alerted on the pool itself: we learned about saturation from failed requests.
- A hotfix was not an option because configuration changes go through the same review as code, which made the rollback the only fast path.
- The release went out in all regions at once; a canary would have limited the impact.
Good. The follow-up ticket for a proper pool sizing is PAY-7712, assigned to omar.s.
Noted: PAY-7712, assigned to omar.s, for a proper card vault pool sizing.
